theory.overview: Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation bridges the gap between interpreted and statically compiled languages. Rather than executing bytecode instruction-by-instruction, the JIT compiler translates hot code paths into native machine code at runtime. This combines the portability of VMs with the speed of native execution. Modern JITs in Java (HotSpot), JavaScript (V8, SpiderMonkey), .NET, and PyPy achieve near-native performance through sophisticated profiling, adaptive optimization, and speculative compilation.

sections.title: The Interpreter-JIT Spectrum
sections.content: Language implementations span a spectrum: pure interpreters (slowest startup, most portable), JIT compilers (balanced), and ahead-of-time compilers (fastest execution, slowest startup). JIT sits in the middle—interpreting initially for fast startup, then compiling hot code for speed. Tiered compilation adds multiple levels: quick baseline JIT for warm code, optimizing JIT for hot code. This balances startup time and peak performance.

spectrum.examples: C, Rust, Go (mostly), GraalVM Native Image

sections.title: Profiling and Hot Spot Detection
sections.content: JITs don't compile everything—they profile to find 'hot' code worth optimizing. Counters track method invocations and loop back-edges. When thresholds are crossed (e.g., 10,000 calls), compilation triggers. Profiling also collects type information: which concrete classes flow through polymorphic call sites, which branches are taken. This data drives speculative optimizations—the JIT optimizes for common cases, inserting guards to fall back if assumptions fail.

sections.title: From Bytecode to Machine Code
sections.content: JIT compilation involves multiple stages: 1) Bytecode parsing and IR (Intermediate Representation) generation, 2) Profiling-guided optimization on IR, 3) Instruction selection (matching IR to CPU instructions), 4) Register allocation (assigning virtual registers to physical ones), 5) Code emission (writing bytes to executable memory). The result is a block of native code that the VM can jump into, with the same semantics as the original bytecode.

sections.title: Key JIT Optimizations
sections.content: JITs perform optimizations impossible for static compilers due to runtime information. Inlining replaces calls with callee body, eliminating call overhead. Devirtualization converts virtual calls to direct calls when type is known constant. Escape analysis identifies objects that don't escape their allocating scope, enabling stack allocation instead of heap. Loop unrolling and vectorization use CPU features. Speculative optimizations assume common paths, with deoptimization guards for rare cases.

optimizations.name: Inlining
optimizations.benefit: Eliminates call overhead, enables further optimizations across calls

optimizations.name: Devirtualization
optimizations.benefit: Direct call instead of virtual dispatch
optimizations.trigger: Monomorphic call site (only one receiver type)

sections.title: Speculation and Deoptimization
sections.content: JITs optimize based on observed behavior, but programs can change. A method seeing only Integers might suddenly receive a Float. The JIT speculatively optimized for Integers, so it inserted a 'guard' (type check). When the guard fails, execution deoptimizes—jumps back to the interpreter or less-optimized code, which handles the general case. The JIT may later recompile with updated profiling data.
process: 1. Profile: Only Integers seen at add() call site
3. Guard: Insert 'if not Integer → deopt' check
6. Re-profile: Now Integers and Floats seen
7. Re-compile: Generic version or dual paths

sections.title: On-Stack Replacement (OSR)
sections.content: What if a long-running loop becomes hot while the method containing it is still executing? OSR solves this: the JIT compiles the loop body and jumps from interpreted code to compiled mid-execution. The stack frame is transformed to match the compiled version's layout, and execution continues in machine code. This ensures even long-running loops get optimized without waiting for method exit.
sections.scenario: Method foo() has a loop running 1M iterations. After 10K iterations, loop becomes hot. OSR compiles loop and switches to native code at iteration 10,001.

keyConcepts.name: Warmup
keyConcepts.description: The period where code runs in interpreter while JIT profiles. Peak performance only after warmup completes.
keyConcepts.benchmarking: Always include warmup iterations in benchmarks

keyConcepts.name: Compilation Threshold
keyConcepts.description: Counter value triggering JIT compilation. Balances compilation overhead vs optimization benefit.
keyConcepts.tuning: Lower for faster compilation, higher for more profiling data

keyConcepts.name: Speculative Optimization
keyConcepts.description: Optimize for observed patterns, with guards for unexpected cases. Enables aggressive optimization of common paths.

keyConcepts.name: Deoptimization
keyConcepts.description: Safely reverting from compiled code to interpreter when assumptions fail. Preserves program correctness.
keyConcepts.mechanism: Guard failure triggers unwind to interpreter state

complexity.compilationTime: $O(codeSize)$ for baseline JIT, $O(codeSize \cdot optimizationDepth)$ for optimizing JIT
complexity.peakPerformance: Near C++ performance for type-stable code

steps.title: Execute in Interpreter
steps.description: Start by interpreting bytecode. Fast startup, immediate execution, while collecting profiling data.

steps.title: Profile Hot Code
steps.description: Increment counters on method entry and loop back-edges. Track types at call sites and branches.

steps.title: Build Intermediate Representation
steps.description: Parse bytecode into IR (often SSA form). IR is platform-independent, enabling optimizations.

steps.title: Optimize IR
steps.description: Apply profiling-guided optimizations: inline hot calls, devirtualize based on type profile, constant fold.

steps.title: Generate Machine Code
steps.description: Lower IR to target CPU instructions, allocate registers, emit binary code to executable memory region.

steps.title: Install and Link
steps.description: Install compiled code in method cache. Future calls jump directly to native code. Insert OSR entry points.

practiceProblems.title: JIT vs Interpreter Speed
practiceProblems.description: Why is JIT-compiled code faster than interpreted bytecode?
practiceProblems.answer: No dispatch overhead, direct CPU execution, optimized machine code with registers
practiceProblems.explanation: Interpreter has dispatch loop overhead per instruction. JIT removes this, uses CPU registers instead of stack, and applies optimizations.

practiceProblems.title: Warmup Period
practiceProblems.description: Why do JIT-based systems need a 'warmup' period to reach peak performance?
practiceProblems.answer: Time needed to profile hot code and compile it to native code
practiceProblems.explanation: Initially everything runs in interpreter. Hot code detection and compilation happens over time. Peak perf only after hot paths are compiled.

practiceProblems.title: Inlining Benefit
practiceProblems.description: What are the benefits of inlining method calls in JIT compilation?
practiceProblems.answer: Eliminates call overhead and enables optimizations across method boundaries
practiceProblems.explanation: Call overhead: save registers, push args, jump, prologue, epilogue, return. Inlining removes all this and lets optimizer work on combined code.

practiceProblems.title: Devirtualization
practiceProblems.description: How does JIT devirtualization work and when can it apply?
practiceProblems.answer: When type profile shows monomorphic call site, convert virtual call to direct call
practiceProblems.explanation: If 100% of calls at a site use class Dog, JIT compiles direct call to Dog.speak() with guard, instead of virtual dispatch table lookup.
hints: Type profile shows single receiver type
Guard for deoptimization if wrong type

practiceProblems.title: Speculative Guard
practiceProblems.description: What is the purpose of 'guards' in speculative JIT compilation?
practiceProblems.answer: Verify assumptions still hold; trigger deoptimization if violated
practiceProblems.explanation: Guard is runtime check: 'if assumption wrong → deoptimize'. Enables aggressive optimization of expected case with safe fallback.

practiceProblems.title: On-Stack Replacement
practiceProblems.description: What problem does On-Stack Replacement (OSR) solve?
practiceProblems.answer: Optimizing long-running loops before method exits
practiceProblems.explanation: Without OSR, hot loop in long method would stay interpreted until method returns. OSR switches to compiled code mid-loop.

practiceProblems.title: Compilation Threshold
practiceProblems.description: Why don't JITs compile code immediately on first execution?
practiceProblems.answer: Compilation overhead exceeds benefit for cold code; profiling needs multiple runs
practiceProblems.explanation: Compiling everything immediately would slow startup. Many methods run only once—interpreting is faster for them. Thresholds ensure we compile only hot code worth optimizing.

practiceProblems.title: Escape Analysis
practiceProblems.description: How does escape analysis enable optimization?
practiceProblems.answer: Objects that don't escape method can be stack-allocated or scalar-replaced, avoiding heap allocation
practiceProblems.explanation: If new Point() is only used locally and not returned/stored globally, JIT can allocate on stack (frees when method returns) or eliminate entirely (scalar replacement).

practiceProblems.title: Deoptimization Cost
practiceProblems.description: What happens when a speculative optimization proves wrong at runtime?
practiceProblems.answer: Execution deoptimizes—jumps to interpreter or less-optimized code. State is reconstructed.
practiceProblems.explanation: Guard fails → unwind to safe point → reconstruct interpreter stack frame → continue in interpreter. Later may recompile with updated profile.

practiceProblems.title: Tiered Compilation
practiceProblems.description: Why do modern VMs use tiered compilation (C1 + C2 in JVM)?
practiceProblems.answer: Balance between quick compilation (C1) and peak performance (C2). C1 for warmup, C2 for hot code.
practiceProblems.explanation: C1 (client) compiles quickly with basic optimizations for decent speed. C2 (server) takes longer but applies aggressive optimizations. Code graduates from interp→C1→C2 based on heat.

minigame.title: Speed Demon JIT
minigame.description: Become a JIT compiler! Profile code, decide what to optimize, and watch your compiled code race against the interpreter. Learn optimization trade-offs and compete on the execution speed leaderboard.
instructions: Watch bytecode execute in the interpreter
Profile to identify hot methods and loops
Balance compilation time vs runtime speed

visualizer.title: JIT Compilation Visualizer
visualizer.description: Watch the JIT compilation pipeline in action. See bytecode transform through IR stages, observe optimization decisions, and compare interpreter vs compiled execution speeds. Profile data drives the visualization.

snippets.title: Simple JIT Concept
snippets.code:
'''Conceptual demo of JIT compilation flow.
Real JITs are complex (thousands of lines).
This shows the key stages conceptually.'''

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, List, Callable, Any
from enum import Enum, auto

class BytecodeOp(Enum):
    LOAD_CONST = auto()
    LOAD_VAR = auto()
    STORE_VAR = auto()
    ADD = auto()
    SUB = auto()
    MUL = auto()
    JUMP = auto()
    JUMP_IF_FALSE = auto()
    CALL = auto()
    RETURN = auto()

@dataclass
class Instruction:
    op: BytecodeOp
    operand: Any = None

# Simulated 'machine code' - actually just Python functions
NativeCode = Callable[[], Any]

class SimpleJIT:
    '''Toy JIT showing compilation stages'''
    
    def __init__(self):
        self.interpreter_counters: Dict[int, int] = {}  # Method IDs
        self.compiled_methods: Dict[int, NativeCode] = {}
        self.COMPILATION_THRESHOLD = 10
    
    def execute_bytecode(self, method_id: int, bytecode: List[Instruction], vars: Dict):
        '''Execute with profiling'''
        
        # Profile: count invocations
        count = self.interpreter_counters.get(method_id, 0) + 1
        self.interpreter_counters[method_id] = count
        
        # Check if we should JIT compile
        if count == self.COMPILATION_THRESHOLD and method_id not in self.compiled_methods:
            print(f'\n[JIT] Method {method_id} reached threshold ({count}), compiling...')
            native_code = self.compile_method(bytecode)
            self.compiled_methods[method_id] = native_code
            print(f'[JIT] Compilation complete! Future calls use native code\n')
        
        # Use compiled version if available
        if method_id in self.compiled_methods:
            print(f'  [NATIVE] Executing compiled code for method {method_id}')
            return self.compiled_methods[method_id]()
        
        # Otherwise interpret
        print(f'  [INTERP] Executing method {method_id} (count={count})')
        return self.interpret(bytecode, vars)
    
    def interpret(self, bytecode: List[Instruction], vars: Dict) -> Any:
        '''Simple stack-based interpreter'''
        pc = 0
        stack = []
        
        while pc < len(bytecode):
            instr = bytecode[pc]
            
            if instr.op == BytecodeOp.LOAD_CONST:
                stack.append(instr.operand)
            elif instr.op == BytecodeOp.LOAD_VAR:
                stack.append(vars.get(instr.operand, 0))
            elif instr.op == BytecodeOp.STORE_VAR:
                vars[instr.operand] = stack.pop()
            elif instr.op == BytecodeOp.ADD:
                b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
                stack.append(a + b)
            elif instr.op == BytecodeOp.SUB:
                b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
                stack.append(a - b)
            elif instr.op == BytecodeOp.MUL:
                b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
                stack.append(a * b)
            elif instr.op == BytecodeOp.RETURN:
                return stack.pop() if stack else None
            
            pc += 1
        
        return None
    
    def compile_method(self, bytecode: List[Instruction]) -> NativeCode:
        '''Toy compiler: creates optimized Python function
        Real JIT would generate machine code'''
        
        # Stage 1: Parse (already have bytecode, create IR conceptually)
        print('  [Stage 1] Bytecode parsed')
        
        # Stage 2: Optimize
        print('  [Stage 2] Applying optimizations:')
        
        # Simple constant folding
        optimized = []
        i = 0
        while i < len(bytecode):
            instr = bytecode[i]
            
            # Constant folding: LOAD_CONST + LOAD_CONST + ADD → LOAD_CONST(result)
            if (i + 2 < len(bytecode) and
                instr.op == BytecodeOp.LOAD_CONST and
                bytecode[i+1].op == BytecodeOp.LOAD_CONST and
                bytecode[i+2].op == BytecodeOp.ADD):
                result = instr.operand + bytecode[i+1].operand
                optimized.append(Instruction(BytecodeOp.LOAD_CONST, result))
                print(f'    - Constant folded: {instr.operand} + {bytecode[i+1].operand} = {result}')
                i += 3
            else:
                optimized.append(instr)
                i += 1
        
        # Stage 3: Code generation (create Python function)
        print('  [Stage 3] Generating native code')
        
        def native_execute():
            '''Simulated 'native' code - actually still Python
            but conceptually this is machine code'''
            # Stack machine simulation but 'optimized'
            stack = []
            for instr in optimized:
                if instr.op == BytecodeOp.LOAD_CONST:
                    stack.append(instr.operand)
                elif instr.op == BytecodeOp.ADD:
                    stack.append(stack.pop() + stack.pop())
                elif instr.op == BytecodeOp.RETURN:
                    return stack[-1] if stack else None
            return stack[-1] if stack else None
        
        return native_execute

# Demo
print('=' * 50)
print('Simple JIT Compilation Demo')
print('=' * 50)

jit = SimpleJIT()

# Simple method: computes 5 + 3 * 2
# Optimized to just return 11 (constant folding)
method_bytecode = [
    Instruction(BytecodeOp.LOAD_CONST, 5),
    Instruction(BytecodeOp.LOAD_CONST, 3),
    Instruction(BytecodeOp.LOAD_CONST, 2),
    Instruction(BytecodeOp.MUL),
    Instruction(BytecodeOp.ADD),
    Instruction(BytecodeOp.RETURN)
]

# Execute multiple times to trigger JIT
for i in range(12):
    result = jit.execute_bytecode(method_id=1, bytecode=method_bytecode, vars={})

print(f'\nFinal result: {result}')
print(f'\nCompiled methods: {list(jit.compiled_methods.keys())}')
print(f'Interpreter invocation counts: {jit.interpreter_counters}')
